chunks.recognized_text: Two cooling towers rise from the wooded hills of Western Washington. They look like a matched pair. Their histories are not. One belonged to Washington Nuclear Project 5. That project was about 14% complete when it was terminated in 1982. The other served Washington Nuclear Project 3. That project reached 74% physical completion and remained preserved for possible completion until 1994. Neither project produced commercial electricity. The site was never fueled. So the mystery is not simply why Satsup was unfinished. It is why two reactor projects built side by side died 12 years apart. And why 74% complete was still too expensive to finish. On January 22nd, 1982, the Washington Public Power Supply System terminated Nuclear Projects 4 and 5. Project 4 stood at Hanford. Project 5 stood here at Satsup. Financial advisors had reached a blunt conclusion. The bond market could not absorb the financing needed to carry all five nuclear projects then being pursued by the supply system. At termination, projects 4 and 5 had sold 2.25 billion dollars in bonds. Their estimated combined completion cost had climbed to roughly 12 billion dollars. About 8.5 billion above the original combined estimate. Project 5 itself was only about 14% complete. The physical project advanced. The estimate for completing projects 4 and 5 had already moved far beyond the original combined plan. But this was not just a construction problem, it was a promise to pay. To see how the region reached that point, rewined 16 years. Through the mid 20th century, federal hydroelectric projects supplied most of the Pacific North West's electricity. By 1966, planners projected demand growing beyond what that system could provide. Utilities in Bonneville organized a regional planning effort. In 1969, that effort adopted a plan calling for several large thermal plants. The supply system moved from a small organization into a builder of 5 nuclear projects. Before 1968, it had fewer than 100 employees. By March 1979, it had 1,471. This was not one isolated plant running over budget. It was an entire portfolio competing for engineering, contractors, equipment, regulatory attention, and financing at the same time. Only one of those 5 projects would eventually operate. Project 2 at Hanford, which entered commercial service in December 1984. By July 1976, 88 customers of the Bonneville Power Administration and one private utility had become participants in projects 4 and 5. The bonds were backed by contracts containing a take or pay obligation. The phrase sounds obscure. It's meaning was painfully clear. Participants were required to pay their share whether the plants were completed, operable, or operating. When the projects were alive, that promise helped make their bonds marketable. Once construction ended, it meant utilities could still face the cost of plants that would never deliver power. GAO reported that rate increases would be required to service the debt. Utilities and ratepayers went to court. The question was no longer only whether the project should continue, it was who would carry the bill after they stopped. On July 22, 1983, the project 4 and 5 bonds went into default. That is the famous the supply system financial collapse. And yet, the neighbouring project at Satsap did not end with it. To understand why, the two towers have to be separated financially. Project 5 belonged to the participant financed Project 4 and 5 system. Project 3 belonged to an earlier group supported through net billing with Bonneville. The federal agency that marketed power from the North West's federal hydroelectric system. Public utilities held capability shares in Project 3 and assigned them to Bonneville. In exchange, Bonneville credited Project costs through their wholesale power bills. 70% of Project 3 used that public net billing structure. For investor owned utilities held the remaining 30%. A later settlement changed Bonneville's exposure and Bonneville ultimately paid all Project 3 Project costs. The structures looked similar because both projects were planned as large, pressurized water reactors of roughly 1240 megawatts. But a cooling tower cannot show who carries the next billion dollars of risk.

chunks.recognized_text: Nor can the tower show how much remained outside it. Each proposed Satsap unit, included a reactor system, auxiliary building, turbine generator, cooling system, transmission connections, and supporting facilities. The tower was the most visible piece, but it was only the heat rejection end of the plant. In operation, reactor heat would produce steam. The steam would spin a turbine generator, and the cooling system would remove waste heat, so water could circulate again. At Satsap, that chain was never completed and never entered service. Project 5 hit its financing wall first. Project 3 had enough support to enter a different state, neither advancing nor dead. Construction on Project 3 was suspended in July 1983. Suspended did not mean terminated. Buildings and installed systems were protected. Equipment and construction materials retained possible value. The option to finish the project remained open. Preservation bought time, it also cost money. Every year changed the calculation. Equipment aged, current regulatory requirements moved. Alternative generating technology improved. The region's demand forecasts changed. The site therefore required work without producing electricity. Preservation meant inspecting what had been built and protecting material that might still be used. It also meant maintaining the option to restart and studying whether that option remained valuable. The longer preservation continued, the more the project faced a paradox. Keeping the option alive required spending money. But spending money to preserve an option did not prove that exercising the option would make sense. By 1994, Bonneville described the project 3 project as 74% physically complete. Approximately 2.6 billion dollars had been invested. Measured in 1993 dollars and including the investor owned utilities share. The cooling tower stood almost 500 feet high. The reactor and turbine buildings existed. From the road, the project could look close to finished. But completion is not measured by how much concrete is visible. It is measured by what still has to be spent and how long that money remains at risk. Most of all, it is measured by whether the electricity will be needed when the plant finally opens. In June 1993, Bonneville began another study of whether project 3 should remain preserved for nuclear completion. The conclusions went before the supply systems executive board in November 1993 and its board of directors in January 1994. The analysis asked for practical questions. Would completion damage Bonneville's competitiveness? Did the region need the power? How did project 3 compare with available alternatives? And what risks came with each choice? This is the human scale centre of the story. The project was no longer an abstract monument. Its remaining cost would flow through institutions to utilities and eventually to the people paying for electricity across the region. Bonneville was already under pressure to control its rates. Its customers were considering other sources of power and some indicated that they might pay a premium for greater independence. Completing project 3 could push Bonneville's costs upward. At the same moment its customers were gaining alternatives. That is how a decision inside a federal power agency reaches a household or a small business. Not as a cooling tower, as a rate. The past 2.6 billion dollars could not answer those questions. That money was already gone. Only the next commitment could still be changed. Bonneville compared project 3 with natural gas combined cycle generation. Plants using gas and steam turbines together. The 1994 exhibits modeled project 3 at 1240 megawatts. The combined cycle reference was 240 megawatts. That difference mattered. Combined cycle resources could be built in smaller increments, letting Bonneville match new supply more closely to actual load growth. Bonneville's assumptions also gave the combined cycle alternative a shorter construction lead time. Three years compared with five years for restarting and completing project 3. The comparison was not one giant replacement plant against one giant nuclear plant. Bonneville could add combined cycle capacity in smaller units as demand appeared. The agency could shape and dispatch that output more flexibly around a hydroelectric system whose generation changed with water conditions. More of a combined cycle plants costs were variable and avoidable when it was not producing power. Project 3 carried a larger share of fixed costs that Bonneville would owe regardless of production.

chunks.recognized_text: The gas option had risks, including fuel prices and possible carbon costs. Bonneville recorded those two. This matters because the 1994 decision was not a claim that combined cycle power was risk-free, or that nuclear generation had no advantages. It was a comparison of which risks Bonneville was willing and able to carry. But it offered something Project 3 could not. Flexibility. An earlier study put the base estimate to complete Project 3 at another $1.55 billion in 1993 dollars. Bonneville also tested lower and higher cases. Combined cycle was cheaper than the base and high Project 3 cases. In the low cost case, Project 3 became comparable over its operating life. But comparable lifetime cost was not enough. In Bonneville's base case, completing Project 3 exposed the agency to nearly three times as much capital at risk as the combined cycle alternative. This comparison measured what would be lost if the resources were terminated early. Even the low Project 3 case carried double the capital at risk. Then came the need question. Bonneville projected that Project 3's full 1240 megawatt output would create about 600 average megawatts of surplus power even under its high load forecast. If all that surplus could be sold at Bonneville's priority firm rate, the agency still estimated a deficit of roughly $200 million per year. The project could work technically and still fail economically. It could generate every megawatt promised and create a financial problem because too much capacity arrived at once. That is what the cooling towers conceal. Mega projects are usually judged by whether engineers can finish them. Project 3 also had to survive a second test whether the system around it could use and pay for what it produced. This was the answer hidden behind the 74% number. The project was mostly built. The region did not need all of its power. And finishing it would concentrate far more capital in one decision than the alternative. Project 3 still had real advantages. Much of it existed. Major sighting permits were in place. Nuclear generation would not face combustion limits on carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide. Bonneville acknowledged those points. It also listed uncertainty in completion cost. Upgrades after years of preservation, operating performance, maintenance, waste, decommissioning, regulation and public opposition. Bonneville examined other possibilities. It considered repowering Project 3 as a gas fired combined cycle plant and found no clear economic advantage over building a new one. It considered whether a third party might use the site. None of those possibilities justified Bonneville continuing to finance preservation for nuclear completion under the existing agreements. In May 1994, the Bonneville Administrator made the final determination. Neither continued preservation nor completion under the existing agreements was in the best interest of Bonneville and the region's ratepayers. Project 3 was terminated in June, not because 74% had disappeared because 74% described the past. The decision had to describe the future. A major project does not end on a single date. Project 5 was terminated in 1982. The project 4 and 5 Bonnes defaulted in 1983. Project 3 construction stopped in 1983. Its completion option ended in 1994. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission revoked its construction permit in January 1999. Property, remediation and debt moved on different schedules. The permit clock asked whether nuclear construction could legally continue. The property clock asked who would own and maintain the buildings. The debt clock followed financing agreements created years earlier. The redevelopment clock asked whether land and infrastructure designed for one purpose could support another. Energy North West, the later name of the supply system, still carried Project 3 debt-related budgeting decades after termination. Its fiscal year 2021 budget covered financing obligations and debt administration, not new construction or plant operation. Concrete is visible. Contracts are not. Both can survive the moment work stops. In 1995, Graze Harbour County, the Port of Graze Harbour, and the local public utility district formed the Satsop redevelopment project. Transfer of the Project 3 property and facilities was completed during fiscal year 2000. The nuclear investment could not be recovered by pretending the reactor still made sense. But parts of the industrial site had value outside the original plan.
